summary: This informational document describes a method that DHCPv6 servers can use to pick semantically opaque IPv6 interface identifiers when leasing non-temporary addresses. It is purely a server-side algorithm and needs no changes to the existing DHCPv6 specifications. The result is addresses that do not reveal information about the client.

plainLanguage.summary: When a hotel hands out room numbers, it could follow a pattern that gives away secrets. This describes a way for the address-giving server to choose addresses that look random and reveal nothing.

questions: how to generate stable private ipv6 addresses in dhcpv6
how does dhcpv6 generate opaque addresses
why are predictable ipv6 addresses a privacy problem
how can i make dhcpv6 addresses unpredictable
subtitle: Generate unpredictable IPv6 addresses on the server side

tldr.problem: When DHCPv6 servers assign IPv6 addresses to clients, the addresses can be predictable, allowing attackers to guess addresses, track devices, or exploit vulnerabilities based on address patterns.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7943 specifies a server-side algorithm that uses a cryptographic hash function (SHA-256 by default) combined with the client's DUID, prefix, and a secret key to generate IPv6 addresses that appear random and cannot be predicted without the secret key.
tldr.outcome: Clients receive stable addresses (consistent within a subnet) that are opaque to outsiders, mitigating address-based location tracking, device fingerprinting, and network reconnaissance attacks.

today: RFC 7943 is an Informational RFC published in September 2016. The IESG noted that it has an unaddressed failure case for address conflicts, but it remains available for implementations seeking privacy-preserving DHCPv6 address assignment.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
DHCPv6 is the protocol that assigns IPv6 addresses to devices on a network. Traditionally, servers could assign addresses in predictable sequences or based on device hardware identifiers. RFC 7943 describes a method for DHCPv6 servers to select semantically opaque interface identifiers (the host portion of the IPv6 address) so that addresses do not reveal information about the client or follow a guessable pattern.

This is a server-side algorithm that requires no changes to existing DHCPv6 specifications or client software. It works by computing a cryptographic hash of the client's DUID (unique identifier), the network prefix, and a secret key known only to the server. The result is an address that is stable (the same client always gets the same address in the same subnet) yet unpredictable to outsiders.
sections.plainLanguage: DHCPv6 is how devices get their IPv6 address from a server. This RFC shows how the server can pick addresses that look random but are actually consistent for each client.

sections.title: Design Goals
sections.content:
RFC 7943 aims to achieve four properties. First, addresses remain stable within each subnet for the same client, even if different DHCPv6 servers (all running this algorithm with the same secret key) assign the address. Second, an attacker cannot predict what address a client will receive without knowing the secret key, even if they know other addresses on the network. Third, addresses remain stable across server reinstallations or loss of the lease database, since they are computed rather than looked up. Fourth, multiple servers can independently generate the same addresses for the same client without sharing state, which simplifies failover scenarios.

The RFC emphasizes that this algorithm only mitigates address-based tracking and device fingerprinting. It does not address all privacy concerns related to DHCPv6, such as the fact that servers can see which clients are requesting addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The goal is addresses that are the same for each client, unpredictable to attackers, and survive server reboots without needing a database.

sections.title: The Algorithm
sections.content:
The algorithm works in four steps. First, compute a random but stable identifier (RID) using a pseudorandom function F. The input includes the network prefix (128-bit), the client's DUID, the IAID (Identity Association Identifier from the DHCPv6 request), a counter starting at 0, and a secret key. The default function is SHA-256, though implementations may offer others. The output must be at least 64 bits.

Second, use the RID to derive a candidate IPv6 address by adding the RID (modulo the address pool size) to the pool's lower boundary. Third, check the resulting address against reserved interface identifiers. If reserved, increment the counter and recompute. Fourth, if the address is already in use (conflicting binding), increment the counter and try again. Through this process, the algorithm naturally handles address conflicts and reserved patterns by simply trying the next value in the sequence determined by the RID.
sections.plainLanguage: Mix the client ID, network prefix, and secret key through a hash function to get a number. Use that number to pick an address from the available range. If someone already has that address, try the next number.

sections.title: Security Parameters
sections.content:
The secret key is the foundation of the algorithm's security. All DHCPv6 servers leasing addresses from the same pool must use the same secret key so they generate the same addresses for the same clients. The key must be kept confidential and should be at least 128 bits long; key lengths of 256 bits are recommended. If an attacker learns the secret key, they can predict all future addresses.

The prefixing of the hash input with the network prefix ensures that different subnets produce different addresses for the same client, which prevents correlation of activities across networks. Including the IAID ensures that different address associations for the same client (e.g., on different interfaces) get different addresses. Implementations MUST provide an interface for administrators to view and change the secret key, and access to it should be restricted (e.g., superuser only) because its secrecy is critical.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret key is like a password the server uses to generate addresses. Bigger keys (256 bits) are better. Different networks get different addresses from the same key.

sections.title: Deployment
sections.content:
This algorithm is purely a server-side decision and requires no changes to clients or to the DHCPv6 specification. An administrator can enable or disable it per server. It works with existing DHCPv6 implementations because it only affects how the server selects which address to offer to a client.

When replacing a DHCPv6 server or reinstalling one, administrators can keep the same secret key to ensure the replacement system generates the same addresses as the original. This is crucial for maintaining stable address assignments across maintenance events. The method is especially useful in scenarios with multiple servers on the same network or embedded devices that cannot maintain a persistent lease database.
sections.plainLanguage: The server can turn this on or off without telling clients anything different. And if the server crashes and restarts, it can still assign the same addresses as before because it just recomputes them.
